title: Projects
text:
Colorado River Hydrology
Analysis of flow trends, peak timing, and predictive modeling at Lees Ferry

Reproducible Workflow: Built a fully transparent and reproducible data pipeline using Quarto, Git, and GitHub Pages.
API Data Ingestion: Mastered the dataRetrieval package to pull live USGS streamflow data for the Colorado River basin.
Hydrologic Time-Series Analysis: Processed daily discharge into Water Year and Seasonal aggregates to analyze long-term trends and the impact of the 21st-century drought.
Visualized: basin-wide trends with a standardized anomaly heatmap and a flow-weighted spatial center analysis
Modeled: the upstream-downstream relationship at the Compact’s accounting point
Evaluated: model assumptions and identified the outlier year the model couldn’t predict

View »


Spacial Analysis: Distances and Projections
Spatial analysis of urban demographic exposure within the 100-mile federal border jurisdiction

Built spatial datasets from three different sources: a CRAN package (tigris), a data package (rnaturalearth), and a downloaded CSV.
Transformed coordinate reference systems and selected a projection appropriate for national-scale distance analysis
Manipulated geometry types — understanding when to use st_union vs. st_combine, and why casting to MULTILINESTRING is required before computing distances to borders
Computed four sets of distances using st_distance() and stored them as labeled unit vectors
Visualized spatial patterns with continuous color scales, gghighlight, and ggrepel
Built an interactive web map using leaflet to present distance data to a general audience

View »


Modifiable areal unit problem - Polygons & Tessellations
Multi-scale assessment of U.S. dam distribution using advanced spatial statistics and custom tessellation workflows

Tessellation Analysis: Optimized spatial support by comparing hexagonal grids and administrative units to minimize geometric bias.
MAUP Mitigation: Quantified the Modifiable Areal Unit Problem to isolate “zoning effects” from true geographic infrastructure density.
Spatial Autocorrelation: Applied Global Moran’s I to identify strong regional clustering across the U.S. dam network.
LISA Hotspot Mapping: Developed Local Indicators of Spatial Association maps to pinpoint critical infrastructure hotspots and spatial outliers.
Operational Insights: Derived actionable management strategies for multi-state coordination based on identified regional clusters.
Reproducible Workflow: Engineered custom R functions to automate spatial joins and statistical classifications for scalable geographic analysis.

View »


Rasters & Remote Sensing
Multi-index ensemble modeling, unsupervised machine learning, and flood extent quantification

Data Transformation: Converted multi-band satellite imagery into a spectral matrix to enable pixel-based statistical analysis.
Unsupervised Learning: Applied the k-means algorithm to group pixels into 12 distinct spectral classes based on their reflectance signatures.
Automated Labeling: Used a contingency table to programmatically identify which k-means cluster most closely aligned with known flood water.
Ensemble Consensus: Summed six different classification methods to create a “certainty map,” highlighting areas where all models agreed on the flood’s extent.
Areal Quantification: Scaled pixel counts by the sensor’s 30m resolution to calculate the total flooded area in square kilometers.

View »


Machine Learning in Hydrology
Spatial cross-validation and predictive modeling of Colorado River Basin hydrologic drivers and streamflow patterns

Spatial Autocorrelation Analysis: Quantified the geographic “signature” of environmental predictors using Moran’s I to identify potential leakage in model training.
Predictor Engineering: Developed a formula focusing on physical drivers while removing coordinate proxies to ensure model transferability.
Advanced Preprocessing: Implemented a robust tidymodels recipe featuring median imputation, log transformations for skewed variables, and normalization.
Machine Learning Benchmarking: Evaluated Random Forest, XGBoost, and Neural Network models, identifying Random Forest as the most robust architecture for regional streamflow prediction.
Model Diagnostics & Tuning: Optimized hyperparameters via space-filling grids and used Variable Importance (VIP) plots to differentiate between physical mechanisms and spatial proxies.

title: About
text:
Hi, I’m Kyle. I’ve always been drawn to the places where people, landscapes, and science overlap. Growing up with a love for the outdoors, I found myself happiest exploring rivers, mountains, and the ecosystems that connect them. That interest eventually guided my academic and professional path from computer science and IT to hands-on fieldwork, outdoor leadership, and now graduate study in Ecosystem Science and Sustainability.
I’m especially passionate about watershed science, water quality, and understanding how ecological processes shape the world we depend on. Whether I’m rafting down the Animas, snowboarding in the San Juans, or working on local conservation projects, I’m constantly inspired by the natural systems I get to study and explore. These experiences motivate me to help protect water resources and support resilient communities in the West.
My work blends analytical thinking with field experience: using data modeling, GIS, and problem-solving to make sense of complex environmental issues, while staying connected to the landscapes I care about through outdoor work and recreation. I’m excited to build a career in water resources, hydrology, or watershed management where I can combine science, technology, and an appreciation for nature.
Outside of school and work, you’ll usually find me snowboarding, rafting, hiking with my dog Summit, or discovering new corners of the Southwest’s diverse ecosystems.
